questions.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2{e}^{t},\,y=2{e}^{-t},\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=-2$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})=2{e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{-t})=-2{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}2{e}^{t}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{-t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+4{e}^{-2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{4({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine $\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t=\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3-{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2}+4t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-{t}^{2})=-2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4t)=2t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{{(-2t)}^{2}+{(2t+4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{16(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\cdot 4\cdot \sqrt{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2{e}^{5t},\,y=5{e}^{2t},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{5t})=10{e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5{e}^{2t})=10{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{5t}\sqrt{{(10{e}^{5t})}^{2}+{(10{e}^{2t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t}\sqrt{100{e}^{10t}+100{e}^{4t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t}\sqrt{100{e}^{4t}({e}^{6t}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t}\cdot \sqrt{100{e}^{4t}}\cdot \sqrt{{e}^{6t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t}\cdot 10{e}^{2t}\cdot \sqrt{{e}^{6t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =40\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{7t}\sqrt{{e}^{6t}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}-2t,\,y=2t-2,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t)=2t-2, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-2)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(2t-2)\sqrt{(2t-2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(2t-2)\sqrt{4(t-1)^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}2(t-1)\cdot 2\sqrt{(t-1)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(t-1)\sqrt{(t-1)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=(t-1)^{2}+1.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2(t-1)\,\text{d}t⟹(t-1)\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{(t-1)^{2}+1}\cdot (t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}[{(2)}^{3/2}-{(1)}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{2}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\pi u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
